title: Micah

stories.title: 🌋 Micah 1
summaryBullets: This is the word of the LORD that came to Micah the Moreshite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah — what he saw regarding Samaria and Jerusalem: (1:1).
Hear, O peoples, all of you; listen, O earth, and everyone in it! May the Lord GOD bear witness against you, the Lord from His holy temple. (1:2).
For behold, the LORD comes forth from His dwelling place; He will come down and tread on the high places of the earth. (1:3).
The mountains will melt beneath Him, and the valleys will split apart, like wax before the fire, like water rushing down a slope. (1:4).
All this is for the transgression of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the high place of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem? (1:5).
Therefore I will make Samaria a heap of rubble in the open field, a planting area for a vineyard. I will pour her stones into the valley and expose her foundations. (1:6).

All her carved images will be smashed to pieces; all her wages will be burned in the fire, and I will destroy all her idols. Since she collected the wages of a prostitute, they will be used again on a prostitute. (1:7).
Because of this I will lament and wail; I will walk barefoot and naked. I will howl like a jackal and mourn like an ostrich. (1:8).
For her wound is incurable; it has reached even Judah; it has approached the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem itself. (1:9).
Do not tell it in Gath; do not weep at all. Roll in the dust in Beth-leaphrah. (1:10).
Depart in shameful nakedness, O dwellers of Shaphir. The dwellers of Zaanan will not come out. Beth-ezel is in mourning; its support is taken from you. (1:11).
For the dwellers of Maroth pined for good, but calamity came down from the LORD, even to the gate of Jerusalem. (1:12).
Harness your chariot horses, O dweller of Lachish. You were the beginning of sin to the Daughter of Zion, for the transgressions of Israel were found in you. (1:13).
Therefore, send farewell gifts to Moresheth-gath; the houses of Achzib will prove deceptive to the kings of Israel. (1:14).
I will again bring a conqueror against you, O dweller of Mareshah. The glory of Israel will come to Adullam. (1:15).
Shave yourselves bald and cut off your hair in mourning for your precious children; make yourselves as bald as an eagle, for they will go from you into exile. (1:16).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 17:5-6: Assyria besieges Samaria for three years, captures it, and deports Israel to Halah, Gozan and the cities of the Medes.
2 Samuel 1:20: David's lament opens with the line Micah reuses, tell it not in Gath, proclaim it not in Ashkelon.
2 Kings 18:13-17: Sennacherib takes the fortified cities of Judah and sends his commanders from Lachish up to Jerusalem.
1 Samuel 22:1-2: David takes refuge in the cave of Adullam and four hundred distressed and indebted men gather to him.
Isaiah 20:2-4: Isaiah walks stripped and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt and Cush.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה ('etnan zonah)
translationNotes.note: 'Etnan is the specific word for a prostitute's fee, and it is used here for the income of Samaria's idol shrines (1:7). Deuteronomy 23:18 bars that money from ever being brought into the house of the LORD. Micah says the silver Samaria collected as a harlot's hire will be stripped off her images and end up paying harlots again.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)
translationNotes.note: The capital of the northern kingdom, built by Omri around 880 BC on a hill he bought for two talents of silver (1 Kings 16:24). It stood alone above the valley, which is why 1:6 pictures its stones poured down the slope and its foundations laid bare. Assyria besieged it three years and deported its people in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5-6), inside Micah's own lifetime.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָכִישׁ (Lakhish)
translationNotes.note: Judah's second city, about 30 miles southwest of Jerusalem, guarding the road up from the coastal plain, and a chariot base, which is why 1:13 tells it to harness the team. Sennacherib stormed it in 701 BC and covered a room of his palace at Nineveh with carved reliefs of the siege, now in the British Museum. The earthen assault ramp his army raised against the southwest corner is still on the site.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹרֶשֶׁת גַּת (Moresheth Gath)
translationNotes.note: Micah's own town (1:1), in the Shephelah, the low chalk hills between the coastal plain and the Judean highlands, near Gath and roughly 25 miles southwest of Jerusalem. Its neighbours in this same list, Lachish, Mareshah and Adullam, all sit in that corridor, which is the ground an army coming up from the coast has to cross. Micah is naming the towns of his own district as the invasion route.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית לְעַפְרָה (Beth le-Aphrah) - שָׁפִיר (Shaphir) - צַאֲנָן (Tsa'anan) - מָרוֹת (Maroth) - לָכִישׁ (Lakhish) - אַכְזִיב (Akhziv) - מָרֵשָׁה (Mareshah)
translationNotes.note: Every town in this list is punned on its own name, and English can carry none of it. Beth-leaphrah means house of dust, so roll in the dust. Shaphir means fair, and its people go by stripped. Tsa'anan sounds like the verb to go out, and its people do not come out. Maroth sounds like bitter, and it waits for good. Lachish sounds like rekhesh, the word for the chariot team it is told to harness. Achzib sounds like akhzav, a wadi that runs dry when you need it. Mareshah sounds like yoresh, the conqueror who takes possession.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶשֶׁר (nesher)
translationNotes.note: Nesher covers both the eagle and the griffon vulture, and the vulture is the bird in view at 1:16 because its head and neck are bare of feathers. Shaving the head was a mourning rite (Job 1:20, Amos 8:10). Walking barefoot and stripped at 1:8 is the same language of grief, and Isaiah 20:2-4 has a prophet doing it as a public sign.

stories.keyTakeaway: Micah declares God's judgment against Samaria and Jerusalem for their idolatry and sin; God will destroy Samaria and the plague of her wickedness will spread to Judah, causing mourning across the towns of Judah as the people go into exile.

stories.title: 🌋 Micah 2
summaryBullets: Woe to those who devise iniquity and plot evil on their beds! At morning’s light they accomplish it because the power is in their hands. (2:1).
They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses. They deprive a man of his home, a fellow man of his inheritance. (2:2).
Therefore this is what the LORD says: “I am planning against this nation a disaster from which you cannot free your necks. Then you will not walk so proudly, for it will be a time of calamity. (2:3).

In that day they will take up a proverb against you and taunt you with this bitter lamentation: ‘We are utterly ruined! He has changed the portion of my people. How He has removed it from me! He has allotted our fields to traitors.’” (2:4).
Therefore, you will have no one in the assembly of the LORD to divide the land by lot. (2:5).
“Do not preach,” they preach. “Do not preach these things; disgrace will not overtake us.” (2:6).
Should it be said, O house of Jacob, “Is the Spirit of the LORD impatient? Are these the things He does?” Do not My words bring good to him who walks uprightly? (2:7).
But of late My people have risen up like an enemy: You strip off the splendid robe from unsuspecting passersby like men returning from battle. (2:8).
You drive the women of My people from their pleasant homes. You take away My blessing from their children forever. (2:9).
Arise and depart, for this is not your place of rest, because its defilement brings destruction— a grievous destruction! (2:10).
If a man of wind were to come and say falsely, “I will preach to you of wine and strong drink,” he would be just the preacher for this people! (2:11).
I will surely gather all of you, O Jacob; I will collect the remnant of Israel. I will bring them together like sheep in a pen, like a flock in the midst of its pasture — a noisy throng. (2:12).
One who breaks open the way will go up before them; they will break through the gate, and go out by it. Their King will pass through before them, the LORD as their leader. (2:13).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 21:1-4: Naboth refuses to sell his vineyard because it is the inheritance of his fathers, and Ahab sulks over it.
Leviticus 25:23-28: Land may not be sold permanently; the nearest kinsman may buy it back and the Jubilee returns it.
Numbers 26:52-56: The land is divided by lot, each tribe receiving its inheritance by the number of its names.
Deuteronomy 5:21: You shall not covet your neighbor's house or field or anything that belongs to him.
Amos 7:12-13: Amaziah orders Amos to stop prophesying at Bethel because it is the king's sanctuary.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָמַד (chamad, covet) - גָּזַל (gazal, tear away by force)
translationNotes.note: Chamad is the verb of the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17) and gazal is armed robbery. Micah puts them in one sentence at 2:2: they covet fields and seize them. Because Leviticus 25 makes a family's field inalienable, taking it is not a hard bargain but the cancelling of a household's standing in Israel. The sentence at 2:4 fits the crime, an enemy parcels out their fields the same way.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחֲלָה (nachalah)
translationNotes.note: Not money left in a will. It is the specific field a family received when Joshua divided Canaan by lot, and a household's living came off it. Leviticus 25:23-28 forbids selling that land permanently, gives the nearest kinsman the right to buy it back, and returns every field to its original family in the Jubilee year. Naboth uses the word when he refuses Ahab in 1 Kings 21:3.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גּוֹרָל (goral, lot) - חֶבֶל (chevel, measuring cord and the plot it measures)
translationNotes.note: Israel's territory was assigned by casting lots, not bought: Numbers 26:55 and Joshua 14:2. A surveyor's cord marked out each family's share, which is why the same Hebrew word means both the cord and the piece of ground. Having no one to cast the line for you in the assembly (2:5) means being struck off the land register.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָטַף (nataph)
translationNotes.note: The verb means to drip or drop, and it is used for prophesying (Amos 7:16, Ezekiel 21:2). At 2:6 the crowd says do not drip and Micah answers that they should not drip, so the line is a sneer at the prophets for dribbling words. At 2:11 he names the preacher they would take: a man dripping wind and lies, promising them wine and beer.

translationNotes.term: Stripping the robe off a passer-by
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂלְמָה (salmah, outer cloak)
translationNotes.note: The salmah was a man's coat by day and his blanket by night, which is why Exodus 22:26-27 and Deuteronomy 24:12-13 order any cloak taken as security for a loan returned before sundown. Pulling it off men walking by in peace (2:8) is that protection turned inside out. Amos 2:8 names the same abuse, men lying down on garments taken in pledge.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַפֹּרֵץ (ha-porets)
translationNotes.note: A title for the one who breaks the wall open so the flock can get out (2:13). The picture in 2:12 is a sheepfold, a stone pen with one narrow gap; the Breaker goes through the barrier first and the penned crowd pours out after him with the LORD at their head.

translationNotes.term: This is not your resting place
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְנוּחָה (menuchah)
translationNotes.note: Menuchah is the settled rest at the end of a journey, and Deuteronomy 12:9 uses it for the land itself, the rest and the inheritance the LORD was giving Israel. At 2:10 Micah tells the men who took other men's fields to get up and go, because this is no longer their resting place. The word turns the promise of Deuteronomy around on them.

stories.keyTakeaway: Micah condemns those who seize fields and houses from their neighbors; the Lord will bring disaster on this people and send them into exile, though he promises to gather a remnant of Jacob like sheep and lead them through the gate.

stories.title: 🏚️ Micah 3
summaryBullets: Then I said: “Hear now, O leaders of Jacob, you rulers of the house of Israel. Should you not know justice? (3:1).
You hate good and love evil. You tear the skin from my people and strip the flesh from their bones. (3:2).
You eat the flesh of my people after stripping off their skin and breaking their bones. You chop them up like flesh for the cooking pot, like meat in a cauldron.” (3:3).
Then they will cry out to the LORD, but He will not answer them. At that time He will hide His face from them because of the evil they have done. (3:4).
This is what the LORD says: “As for the prophets who lead My people astray, who proclaim peace while they chew with their teeth, but declare war against one who puts nothing in their mouths: (3:5).
Therefore night will come over you without visions, and darkness without divination. The sun will set on these prophets, and the daylight will turn black over them. (3:6).
Then the seers will be ashamed and the diviners will be disgraced. They will all cover their mouths because there is no answer from God.” (3:7).
As for me, however, I am filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin. (3:8).
Now hear this, O leaders of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel, who despise justice and pervert all that is right, (3:9).
who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with iniquity. (3:10).

Her leaders judge for a bribe, her priests teach for a price, and her prophets practice divination for money. Yet they lean upon the LORD, saying, “Is not the LORD among us? No disaster can come upon us.” (3:11).
Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple mount a wooded ridge. (3:12).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 26:18: Micah 3:12 quoted in Hezekiah’s time.
Ezekiel 22:27-29: Princes, priests, and prophets devour and extort.
Matthew 23:23: Justice, mercy, and faithfulness neglected (later rebuke).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָסַם (qāsam), Greek (LXX): μαντεύομαι, Aramaic: קְסָם
translationNotes.note: Forbidden practice tied to paid oracles (3:11). Micah contrasts this with true word from God.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁחַד (shochad)
translationNotes.note: A payment to a judge to bend a verdict. The law bans it in the same words twice, that a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19), and Deuteronomy 27:25 puts a public curse on anyone who takes one to kill an innocent man. Micah 3:11 says Jerusalem's judges took bribes openly and still said the LORD was among them.

translationNotes.term: Priests who teach for a price
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּמְחִיר יוֹרוּ (bimchir yoru, they teach for a price)
translationNotes.note: Teaching the law was part of a priest's job, not a service for sale (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10). Priests were given no tribal land and lived on the tithes and assigned portions of the offerings instead (Numbers 18:20-21), so they were already provided for. Charging for a ruling meant the ruling went to whoever paid.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִיּוֹן שָׂדֶה תֵחָרֵשׁ (tsiyyon sadeh techaresh)
translationNotes.note: This sentence was still being quoted roughly a century later. In Jeremiah 26:17-19 the elders of Judah name Micah the Moreshite, repeat this verse word for word, and point out that Hezekiah did not put him to death for saying it. The quotation is what kept Jeremiah from being executed.

stories.keyTakeaway: God denounces murderous injustice and pay-for-prophecy. The city that trusts in status and money is warned it will be leveled.

stories.title: 🏔️ Micah 4
summaryBullets: In the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills, and the peoples will stream to it. (4:1).

And many nations will come and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob. He will teach us His ways, so that we may walk in His paths.” For the law will go forth from Zion and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem. (4:2).

Then He will judge between many peoples and arbitrate for strong nations far and wide. Then they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor will they train anymore for war. (4:3).
And each man will sit under his own vine and under his own fig tree, with no one to frighten him. For the mouth of the LORD of Hosts has spoken. (4:4).
Though all the nations may walk in the name of their gods, yet we will walk in the name of the LORD our God forever and ever. (4:5).
“On that day,” declares the LORD, “I will gather the lame; I will assemble the outcast, even those whom I have afflicted. (4:6).
And I will make the lame into a remnant, the outcast into a strong nation. Then the LORD will rule over them in Mount Zion from that day and forever. (4:7).
And you, O watchtower of the flock, O stronghold of the Daughter of Zion — the former dominion will be restored to you; sovereignty will come to the Daughter of Jerusalem.” (4:8).
Why do you now cry aloud? Is there no king among you? Has your counselor perished so that anguish grips you like a woman in labor? (4:9).

Writhe in agony, O Daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor. For now you will leave the city and camp in the open fields. You will go to Babylon; there you will be rescued; there the LORD will redeem you from the hand of your enemies! (4:10).
But now many nations have assembled against you, saying, “Let her be defiled, and let us feast our eyes on Zion.” (4:11).
But they do not know the thoughts of the LORD or understand His plan, for He has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor. (4:12).

Rise and thresh, O Daughter of Zion, for I will give you horns of iron and hooves of bronze to break to pieces many peoples. Then you will devote their gain to the LORD, their wealth to the Lord of all the earth. (4:13).
crossRefs: Isaiah 2:2-4: Parallel oracle about Zion and peace.
Zechariah 3:10: Vine-and-fig-tree peace image.
Psalm 46:9: He makes wars cease.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַרְבוֹת→אִתִּים; חֲנִיתוֹת→מַזְמֵרוֹת, Greek (LXX): μάχαιραι→ἄροτρα; λόγχαι→δρέπανα, Aramaic: סייפין→אתין; רומחין→מזמרין
translationNotes.note: Weapon-to-tool reversal signals an end to warfare (4:3).

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּרֶן (goren)

translationNotes.term: His own vine and fig tree
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּחַת גַּפְנוֹ וְתַחַת תְּאֵנָתוֹ (tachat gafno v'tachat te'enato)
translationNotes.note: A fixed phrase for a man secure on his own ground, not a picture of leisure. Vines and fig trees take years to come into bearing, so sitting under your own means no army has burned them and no creditor has taken them. 1 Kings 4:25 uses it of Solomon's reign from Dan to Beersheba, and in 2 Kings 18:31 the Assyrian field commander dangles it in front of Jerusalem as the payoff for surrender.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִגְדַּל־עֵדֶר (Migdal Eder, tower of the flock)
translationNotes.note: A stone tower raised in open pasture so a shepherd could see over the flock, keep watch through the night, and sleep off the ground. Genesis 35:21 places one by that name on Jacob's road south, past Bethlehem. Micah 4:8 sets the title beside stronghold of the Daughter of Zion.

Micah 4:1-3 and Isaiah 2:2-4 run almost word for word: the mountain of the LORD's house raised above the hills, nations streaming to it, the law going out from Zion, swords beaten into plowshares. The two men prophesied in Judah at the same time, Micah under Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1) and Isaiah under Uzziah and those same three kings (Isaiah 1:1).

stories.keyTakeaway: God pictures a future where His instruction brings justice, disarmament, and secure daily life.

headings.text: The Mountain of the House of the Lord

stories.title: 👑 Micah 5
summaryBullets: Now, O daughter of troops, mobilize your troops; for a siege is laid against us! With a rod they will strike the cheek of the judge of Israel. (5:1).
But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel— One whose origins are of old, from the days of eternity. (5:2).
Therefore Israel will be abandoned until she who is in labor has given birth; then the rest of His brothers will return to the children of Israel. (5:3).

He will stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majestic name of the LORD His God. And they will dwell securely, for then His greatness will extend to the ends of the earth. (5:4).
And He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land and tramples our citadels. We will raise against it seven shepherds, even eight leaders of men. (5:5).
And they will rule the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod with the blade drawn. So He will deliver us when Assyria invades our land and marches into our borders. (5:6).
Then the remnant of Jacob will be in the midst of many peoples like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass, which do not wait for man or linger for mankind. (5:7).

Then the remnant of Jacob will be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, like a young lion among flocks of sheep, which tramples and tears as it passes through, with no one to rescue them. (5:8).
Your hand will be lifted over your foes, and all your enemies will be cut off. (5:9).
“In that day,” declares the LORD, “I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots. (5:10).
I will remove the cities of your land and tear down all your strongholds. (5:11).
I will cut the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers. (5:12).
I will also cut off the carved images and sacred pillars from among you, so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands. (5:13).
I will root out the Asherah poles from your midst and demolish your cities. (5:14).
I will take vengeance in anger and wrath upon the nations that have not obeyed Me.” (5:15).
crossRefs: Ruth 4:11: Bethlehem/Ephrathah named (family/district).
Matthew 2:5-6: Bethlehem citation in later narrative.
2 Samuel 5:2: Shepherd-king language for Israel’s ruler.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית לֶחֶם אֶפְרָתָה, Greek (LXX): Βηθλεὲμ Ἐφραθά, Aramaic: בית לחם אפרתא
translationNotes.note: Ephrathah identifies the district/family line around Bethlehem (5:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִקֶּדֶם מִימֵי עוֹלָם, Greek (LXX): ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς ἐξ ἡμερῶν αἰῶνος, Aramaic: מן לקדמין מן יומי עלמא
translationNotes.note: Idiomatic phrase for antiquity; Micah states it without framing an interpretation (5:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁבְעָה רֹעִים… שְׁמֹנָה נְסִיכֵי אָדָם, Greek (LXX): ἑπτὰ ποιμένες… ὀκτὼ ἄρχοντες, Aramaic: שבעה רועין… תמניא נסיכי אנש
translationNotes.note: Laddered-number idiom for ample/comprehensive leadership (5:5).

stories.keyTakeaway: God promises rescue out of pain, a ruler from Bethlehem who shepherds in strength, and ample leadership to face invaders.

stories.title: ⚖️ Micah 6
summaryBullets: Hear now what the LORD says: “Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. (6:1).
Hear, O mountains, the LORD’s indictment, you enduring foundations of the earth. For the LORD has a case against His people, and He will argue it against Israel: (6:2).
‘My people, what have I done to you? Testify against Me how I have wearied you! (6:3).
For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery. I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam. (6:4).

My people, remember what Balak king of Moab counseled and what Balaam son of Beor answered. Remember your journey from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you may acknowledge the righteousness of the LORD.’” (6:5).
With what shall I come before the LORD when I bow before the God on high? Should I come to Him with burnt offerings, with year-old calves? (6:6).
Would the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousand rivers of oil? Shall I present my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? (6:7).
He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God? (6:8).
The voice of the LORD calls out to the city (and it is sound wisdom to fear Your name): “Heed the rod and the One who ordained it. (6:9).
Can I forget any longer, O house of the wicked, the treasures of wickedness and the short ephah, which is accursed? (6:10).
Can I excuse dishonest scales or bags of false weights? (6:11).
For the wealthy of the city are full of violence, and its residents speak lies; their tongues are deceitful in their mouths. (6:12).
Therefore I am striking you severely, to ruin you because of your sins. (6:13).
You will eat but not be satisfied, and your hunger will remain with you. What you acquire, you will not preserve; and what you save, I will give to the sword. (6:14).
You will sow but not reap; you will press olives but not anoint yourselves with oil; you will tread grapes but not drink the wine. (6:15).

You have kept the statutes of Omri and all the practices of Ahab’s house; you have followed their counsel. Therefore I will make you a desolation, and your inhabitants an object of contempt; you will bear the scorn of the nations.” (6:16).
crossRefs: Numbers 22:1-6: Balak king of Moab sends to Pethor for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel.
Joshua 4:19-20: Israel crosses the Jordan and camps at Gilgal, where Joshua sets up the twelve stones.
Amos 8:4-6: Traders shrink the ephah, inflate the shekel, rig the scales, and buy the poor for silver.
1 Kings 16:23-33: Omri buys the hill of Samaria and his son Ahab builds a temple of Baal and sets up an Asherah pole.
2 Kings 16:3: Ahaz king of Judah sacrificed his own son in the fire, following the practice of the nations.

translationNotes.term: Balak and Balaam, Shittim to Gilgal
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִן־הַשִּׁטִּים עַד־הַגִּלְגָּל (min ha-Shittim ad ha-Gilgal)
translationNotes.note: At 6:5 the LORD's case points to two things the reader is expected already to know. Balak king of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel and the curse kept coming out as blessing (Numbers 22-24). Shittim was the last camp east of the Jordan (Numbers 25:1) and Gilgal the first camp west of it (Joshua 4:19), so the two names are the start and the end of the crossing into the land.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּכוֹרִי (bekhori, my firstborn) - פְּרִי בִטְנִי (peri vitni, the fruit of my body)
translationNotes.note: 6:7 climbs a ladder of offerings, calves, then thousands of rams, then ten thousand rivers of oil, and ends at burning a child. That was a live practice in the region and not a figure of speech: 2 Kings 3:27 has the king of Moab offer his eldest son on the wall, and 2 Kings 16:3 and 21:6 record kings of Judah passing their own sons through the fire. The law bans it outright at Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2-5.

translationNotes.term: Ten thousands of rivers of oil
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רִבְבוֹת נַחֲלֵי־שָׁמֶן (rivevot nachale shamen)
translationNotes.note: Revavah is the Hebrew for ten thousand and stands for any uncountable amount. Olive oil was pressed by the jar and stored by the jar, never by the streambed, so 6:7 is offering a physical impossibility on purpose. Each rung of the ladder costs more, and the answer at 6:8 costs nothing and is the one thing not offered.

translationNotes.term: Do justice, love loyal love, walk humbly
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט (asot mishpat) - אַהֲבַת חֶסֶד (ahavat chesed) - הַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת (hatsnea lekhet)
translationNotes.note: Mishpat is the court's verdict, what a judge is supposed to hand down. Chesed is loyalty inside a covenant, the faithfulness owed to someone you are bound to, which is why both mercy and steadfast love render it. Hatsnea lekhet is to walk close in, without display. The three answer the sacrifices piled up in 6:6-7.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵיפַת רָזוֹן (eiphat razon, a wasted ephah)
translationNotes.note: The ephah was the standard dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts, the amount Ruth carried home after a day of gleaning (Ruth 2:17). A short ephah is a scoop cut down so the seller hands over less than he charges for (6:10). Leviticus 19:35-36 and Deuteronomy 25:14-15 require a full measure by name, and Amos 8:5 catches merchants at the same trick.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹאזְנֵי רֶשַׁע (mozne resha) - אַבְנֵי מִרְמָה (avne mirmah, stones of deceit)
translationNotes.note: Weights were cut stones carried in a pouch, and 6:11 pictures a bag of them. The fraud was simple: keep two sets, a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling. Deuteronomy 25:13 forbids exactly that, two kinds of weight in your bag, a large and a small, and Proverbs 20:23 calls a false balance no good thing.

translationNotes.term: Statutes of Omri, works of the house of Ahab
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֻקּוֹת עָמְרִי (chuqqot Omri) - מַעֲשֵׂה בֵית־אַחְאָב (ma'aseh veth Achav)
translationNotes.note: Omri founded Samaria, and his son Ahab married Jezebel of Sidon and built a temple of Baal in it (1 Kings 16:23-33). Their policy is the standard 6:16 measures Judah against, a century later and in the southern kingdom, which is the sting. Omri was known outside Israel too; Assyrian records went on calling the northern kingdom the house of Omri for generations after his line ended.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD calls the mountains to witness his accusation against Israel, reminding them of his past acts and asking what offering they think will satisfy him; he tells them he requires justice, mercy, and humility, then pronounces judgment on their dishonest dealings and empty harvests because they have followed the evil ways of Omri and Ahab.

stories.title: ⚖️ Micah 7
summaryBullets: Woe is me! For I am like one gathering summer fruit at the gleaning of the vineyard; there is no cluster to eat, no early fig that I crave. (7:1).
The godly man has perished from the earth; there is no one upright among men. They all lie in wait for blood; they hunt one another with a net. (7:2).
Both hands are skilled at evil; the prince and the judge demand a bribe. When the powerful utters his evil desire, they all conspire together. (7:3).
The best of them is like a brier; the most upright is sharper than a hedge of thorns. The day for your watchmen has come, the day of your visitation. Now is the time of their confusion. (7:4).
Do not rely on a friend; do not trust in a companion. Seal the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms. (7:5).
For a son dishonors his father, a daughter rises against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. A man’s enemies are the members of his own household. (7:6).
But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation. My God will hear me. (7:7).
Do not gloat over me, my enemy! Though I have fallen, I will arise; though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light. (7:8).
Because I have sinned against Him, I must endure the rage of the LORD, until He argues my case and executes justice for me. He will bring me into the light; I will see His righteousness. (7:9).
Then my enemy will see and will be covered with shame — she who said to me, “Where is the LORD your God?” My eyes will see her; at that time she will be trampled like mud in the streets. (7:10).
The day for rebuilding your walls will come — the day for extending your boundary. (7:11).
On that day they will come to you from Assyria and the cities of Egypt, even from Egypt to the Euphrates, from sea to sea and mountain to mountain. (7:12).
Then the earth will become desolate because of its inhabitants, as the fruit of their deeds. (7:13).
Shepherd with Your staff Your people, the flock of Your inheritance. They live alone in a woodland, surrounded by pastures. Let them graze in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old. (7:14).
As in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show My wonders. (7:15).
Nations will see and be ashamed, deprived of all their might. They will put their hands over their mouths, and their ears will become deaf. (7:16).

They will lick the dust like a snake, like reptiles slithering on the ground. They will come trembling from their strongholds in the presence of the LORD our God; they will tremble in fear of You. (7:17).

Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance — who does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in loving devotion? (7:18).
He will again have compassion on us; He will vanquish our iniquities. You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea. (7:19).
You will show faithfulness to Jacob and loving devotion to Abraham, as You swore to our fathers from the days of old. (7:20).
crossRefs: Leviticus 19:9-10: Do not strip your vineyard bare or gather its fallen grapes, but leave them for the poor and the foreigner.
Psalm 42:3: Men taunt the psalmist all day long by asking where his God is.
Matthew 10:35-36: Jesus quotes this chapter, that a man's enemies will be the members of his own household.
Exodus 34:6-7: The LORD proclaims Himself compassionate and gracious, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin.
Genesis 28:13-15: At Bethel the LORD swears to Jacob to give him the land and to bring him back to it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹלְלֹת (olelot, the grapes left after the picking)
translationNotes.note: 7:1 is a man walking a vineyard after harvest with nothing left to eat. Leviticus 19:10 and Deuteronomy 24:21 forbid a grower to strip his vines twice; what the pickers miss belongs to the poor and the foreigner, and Ruth 2 shows the practice running in a barley field. So the picture is ground already gone over by the owner and then by the gleaners, and Micah says even that is bare.

translationNotes.term: A man's enemies are in his own house
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֹיְבֵי אִישׁ אַנְשֵׁי בֵיתוֹ (oyeve ish anshe veto)
translationNotes.note: 7:6 lists son against father, daughter against mother, daughter-in-law against mother-in-law. Households in Israel were extended and shared one walled compound, one courtyard and one income, so these are people who cannot get away from each other. Jesus quotes the verse almost word for word at Matthew 10:35-36, and Luke 12:53 repeats it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַנָּהָר (ha-nahar, the River)
translationNotes.note: The River with no name attached always means the Euphrates (Genesis 15:18, Joshua 1:4). 7:12 sweeps from Assyria in the northeast to the fortified cities of Egypt in the southwest and back again to the Euphrates: the two empires that squeezed Judah between them, named here as the countries the scattered will come home from.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּשָׁן (Bashan) - גִּלְעָד (Gil'ad)
translationNotes.note: Both lie east of the Jordan and both were grazing country, which is why 7:14 asks for the flock to feed there. Bashan is the high volcanic plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, so rich that its cattle and its oaks became proverbs (Amos 4:1, Isaiah 2:13). Gilead is the wooded highland south of it, known for its balm (Jeremiah 8:22). Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria took both and deported the people in 733 BC (2 Kings 15:29).

translationNotes.term: Lick the dust like a serpent
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְלַחֲכוּ עָפָר כַּנָּחָשׁ (yelachaku aphar ka-nachash)
translationNotes.note: Going face down on the ground, as at 7:17, was the required posture before a great king in Assyria and Persia, and Assyrian palace reliefs show beaten rulers doing it in front of the throne. The same image of enemies licking dust appears at Psalm 72:9 and Isaiah 49:23. Comparing it to the serpent points back to Genesis 3:14, where dust is what the serpent is sentenced to eat.

translationNotes.term: Who is a God like You
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִי־אֵל כָּמוֹךָ (mi El kamokha) - מִיכָה (Mikhah)
translationNotes.note: The prophet's name is a question. Mikhah is the short form of Mikhayahu, who is like Yah. At 7:18 the book asks it out loud, mi El kamokha, who is a God like you. English cannot show that the closing movement of the book is built on the writer's own name.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְצֻלוֹת יָם (metsulot yam)
translationNotes.note: Metsulah is deep water a man cannot stand in and cannot recover anything from. The same phrase is where Pharaoh's chariots went down at Exodus 15:5, so when 7:19 hurls our sins into the depths of the sea it is using the exodus wording for something drowned and gone. 7:20 then names the oath sworn to Abraham and Jacob as the reason.

stories.keyTakeaway: Micah laments the moral collapse of society where no righteous person remains and corruption rules; yet he expresses confidence that God will vindicate him and eventually restore and show mercy to his people.

intro:
Micah was written by Micah of Moresheth (Micah 1:1), the prophet from Moresheth-Gath in the Shephelah of Judah, during the reigns of three Judahite kings: Jotham (750-732 BC), Ahaz (735-715 BC), and Hezekiah (715-686 BC). His ministry spanned roughly forty years, from about 740 BC to 686 BC. Micah was from Moresheth-Gath (Micah 1:1, 14), a small farming town in the rolling Shephelah hills about twenty-five miles southwest of Jerusalem, near the Philistine border (the site is identified with Tel Goded / Tell ej-Judeideh). Unlike Isaiah, who came from the royal court in Jerusalem, Micah was a rural prophet from the agricultural margins of Judah, which colored his denunciations of urban corruption and the dispossession of small landowners (Micah 2:1-2). The prophet's name Mikha (מִיכָה) is a shortened form of Mikhayahu (מִיכָיָהוּ), meaning "Who is like Yahuah?" The name was common in ancient Israel: other Micahs and Micaiahs in the Old Testament include Micah the Ephraimite who set up an idol-house with a Levite priest (Judges 17-18), Micaiah son of Imlah (a different prophet who confronted King Ahab of Israel, 1 Kings 22; 2 Chronicles 18), and several others; none of these are identical with Micah of Moresheth. Jeremiah 26:17-19 explicitly references Micah's ministry a century later and quotes Micah 3:12, attesting that "Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah" and that his preaching had led King Hezekiah to repentance.

The historical setting is the second half of the eighth century BC, during the rise of the Neo-Assyrian Empire to dominance over the ancient Near East. Tiglath-Pileser III (745-727 BC) had reorganized Assyria's military and administrative systems for the conquest of the Levant; he campaigned through Syria and Israel, eventually deporting populations from the northern Transjordan. Shalmaneser V (727-722 BC) besieged Samaria; Sargon II (722-705 BC) completed the conquest of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and deported the ten northern tribes. Sennacherib (705-681 BC) invaded Judah in 701 BC, captured all the fortified cities of the Shephelah (including the major city of Lachish, eight miles from Micah's hometown of Moresheth-Gath), and besieged Jerusalem under King Hezekiah. The siege was lifted after a divinely-sent plague struck the Assyrian army (2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36; 2 Chronicles 32:21; corroborated indirectly by Sennacherib's own Taylor Prism inscription, which boasts of shutting Hezekiah "like a bird in a cage" without claiming the city's capture). Micah's contemporaries included Isaiah of Jerusalem (the royal-court prophet) and the slightly older northern prophets Hosea and Amos. Egypt under the 25th Dynasty (the Kushite or Ethiopian Pharaohs) attempted to support Judah against Assyria but was repeatedly defeated.

Micah is the thirty-third book of the Christian Old Testament and the sixth of the twelve Minor Prophets. The Hebrew name Mikhah (מִיכָה) is the prophet's own name. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Micah were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; the Wadi Murabba'at Minor Prophets scroll (Mur 88), discovered in caves near Qumran in 1955 and dated to the 1st-2nd century AD, preserves the Hebrew text of Micah substantially intact and matches the later Masoretic Text closely. Matthew 2:5-6 quotes Micah 5:2 as the prophecy fulfilled by Jesus' birth in Bethlehem: "And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel." Micah's swords-into-plowshares vision (Micah 4:1-4) is also closely paralleled in Isaiah 2:2-4, the two prophets sharing the same restoration oracle.
